items.title: NASA begins Artemis 2 countdown after cold weather delay

featured_image.name: NASA delays the first Artemis moonshot with astronauts ...

items.description:
A rare arctic outbreak sweeping through Florida has forced NASA to postpone the first crewed lunar mission in more than half a century, tightening an already narrow launch window for the Artemis II mission.

NASA announced Friday that the first possible launch date for Artemis II is now no earlier than February 8, two days later than originally planned, after sub-freezing temperatures at Kennedy Space Center made a critical fueling test impossible to conduct this weekend. The agency had intended to perform the "wet dress rehearsal" of its 322-foot Space Launch System rocket on Saturday but canceled the operation late Thursday.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Danish veterans march on US embassy over Trump NATO remarks

featured_image.name: Denmark: Thousands take part in veteran anti-Trump protest

items.description:
Veterans and officials throughout the NATO alliance have reacted with fury to President Donald Trump's claim that allied forces "stayed a little back, a little off the front lines" during the Afghanistan War, with Danish veterans organizing a protest march on the US embassy in Copenhagen on Saturday.

Trump sparked the controversy during a January 22 interview with Fox News in Davos, Switzerland, questioning NATO's reliability and asserting that the United States had "never needed" its allies. "We have never really asked anything of them," Trump said. "They'll say they sent some troops to Afghanistan or this or that. And they did — they stayed a little back, a little off the front lines."[1][2]

The remarks drew immediate backlash given that 457 British, 158 Canadian, and 44 Danish service members were killed during the two-decade Afghanistan conflict — after NATO invoked Article 5, its mutual defense clause, for the first and only time following the September 11 attacks.[3][4]

featured_image.name: The CEO Steering Hyundai's $26 Billion U.S. Bet—and Its Push ...

items.description:
José Muñoz, the first non-Korean leader of any major Korean conglomerate, is doubling down on America even as tariffs and shifting electric vehicle policies roil the auto industry.

In an interview with The Wall Street Journal released Friday, the Hyundai Motor president and CEO outlined his vision to localize production and deploy humanoid robots as the South Korean automaker navigates trade tensions with Washington.[1][2]

"America is the most important market for Hyundai," Muñoz said, adding that the company wants "at least 80% of what we sell in the US" to be produced domestically. "This is the best recipe to be successful and to not be dependent on policies."[2]

Alphabet Inc.'s autonomous driving unit Waymo is aiming to raise about $16 billion in a financing round that would value the robotaxi company at nearly $110 billion, according to people familiar with the matter, as reported by Bloomberg News on Saturday.[1][2][3]

items.title: Ukraine grid failure triggers Chornobyl power loss, blackouts

featured_image.name: IAEA flags damage to Chornobyl nuclear plant’s protective shield in Ukraine

items.description:
Ukrainian nuclear power plants temporarily reduced their output Saturday morning after a technical malfunction triggered a cascading failure across the country's power grid, forcing Chornobyl to briefly lose all off-site power, the International Atomic Energy Agency reported.

The disruption, which also caused widespread blackouts in neighboring Moldova, struck at 10:42 a.m. local time when a 750-kilovolt line between western and central Ukraine and a 400-kilovolt line connecting Romania and Moldova simultaneously shut down, according to Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal. The failure activated automatic protection systems at substations and forced nuclear plant units to unload their power, leading to emergency outages across multiple regions including Kyiv and Kharkiv.[1][2][3][4][5][6]

items.title: Japan, UK launch cyber partnership amid China tensions
items.description:
Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and British Prime Minister Keir Starmer agreed Saturday to deepen cooperation on cybersecurity, defense, and critical mineral supply chains during talks in Tokyo, as both nations seek to counter China's growing influence in the Indo-Pacific region.

The summit at the Prime Minister's Office concluded with the announcement of a new Japan-UK Strategic Cyber Partnership aimed at detecting, deterring, and defending against cyber threats from foreign adversaries. The two leaders also affirmed the urgent need for like-minded nations to strengthen supply chains for essential minerals, with China's recent export restrictions on rare earth elements adding urgency to the discussions.[1][2][3][4]

items.title: Particle accelerator decodes lost ancient Greek star catalog

featured_image.name: Lost ancient Greek star catalog decoded by particle accelerator

items.description:
Powerful X-rays from a particle accelerator have illuminated fragments of one of history's most important astronomical documents—the lost star catalog of the ancient Greek astronomer Hipparchus—after lying hidden beneath medieval religious texts for more than a millennium.

Researchers working at SLAC National Accelerator Laboratory in Menlo Park, California, this month successfully decoded erased ancient Greek text from a manuscript known as the Codex Climaci Rescriptus, including star coordinates that date back more than 2,000 years.[1][2][3]

items.title: Interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS nears Jupiter flyby after archival data reveals early presence

featured_image.name: Water on interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS glows in ultraviolet light

items.description:
Scientists have confirmed that the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS was captured in space-based observations nearly two months before its official discovery on July 1, 2025, underscoring questions about how automated detection systems process vast astronomical datasets. The revelation comes as the interstellar visitor approaches a close pass with Jupiter in mid-March that researchers say could expose new secrets about its composition and structure.

According to newly confirmed analyses, 3I/ATLAS appeared in data collected by NASA's Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) between May 7 and June 2, 2025—55 days before the ATLAS telescope in Chile flagged the object as a potential interstellar visitor. The comet remained effectively invisible in those earlier recordings until scientists revisited the data with updated parameters and image-stacking techniques, coadding more than 9,000 individual frames to reconstruct a faint but consistent signal matching the object's trajectory.[1][2][3]

items.title: Scientists engineer bacteria to produce molecules using light

featured_image.name: Light-Driven Method Boosts Eco-Friendly Biomanufacturing with ...

items.description:
Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign have engineered bacteria that can manufacture novel molecules when activated by light, marking what scientists describe as the first integration of light-driven enzymatic reactions into cellular metabolism. The proof-of-concept study, published this week in Nature Catalysis, could expand the range of compounds that can be sustainably produced through biomanufacturing.[1][2][3]

The technology works by equipping Escherichia coli bacteria with artificial photoenzymes—light-activated catalysts capable of performing chemical reactions that natural enzymes cannot achieve. When illuminated, these engineered bacteria can convert glucose into higher-value chemical products without requiring costly external materials.[4][1]

items.title: NASA confirms 3I/ATLAS was in its data months before discovery

featured_image.name: NASA’s TESS Captures First Images of Rare Interstellar Comet 3I/ATLAS

items.description:
Seven months after the discovery of interstellar object 3I/ATLAS, NASA has confirmed that the comet was captured in observational datasets dating back to May 2025—almost two months before astronomers identified it as a visitor from another star system. The revelation is prompting renewed scrutiny of planetary defense detection capabilities.

According to peer-reviewed research and NASA statements, the Transiting Exoplanet Survey Satellite (TESS) recorded the comet nearly continuously from May 7 to June 2, 2025—55 days before its official discovery on July 1, 2025. The object was too faint to be detected in individual 200-second TESS exposures, and only became visible when researchers retroactively stacked thousands of images after learning where to look.[1][2][3][4]

"The mission's wide field of view previously happened to observe 3I/ATLAS in May 2025, almost two months before it was discovered," NASA stated in a January 27 blog post announcing new TESS observations of the comet. "Astronomers looking back at the TESS data were able to identify the faint comet by stacking multiple observations to track its movement."[5]
